subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: If f, given by f(x) = k²x − k for x ≥ 1 and f(x) = 2 for x < 1, is a continuous function on ℝ, then find the values of k.

mark_split.label: Name the only point that needs checking
Write the two one-sided limits and f(1)
Match the two pieces at x = 1

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say which single point decides it, and what equation in k you would end up solving.

steps.label: Name the only point that needs checking
steps.margin_note: First mark. Continuity is given, k is not — so the work runs backwards. Say why only x = 1 matters: away from 1 each piece is a constant or a polynomial, and those are continuous for every k.
steps.memory_tip: For a two-piece function, every value of k is safe except at the join — so the join is the only equation you ever get.
lines: Given f(x) = k²x − k   for x ≥ 1,   and f(x) = 2   for x < 1
For x < 1, f is the constant 2, which is continuous for every value of k.
For x > 1, f is the polynomial k²x − k, which is continuous for every value of k.
So f can fail to be continuous only where the two pieces meet, at x = 1.
f is continuous on ℝ ⇒ f is continuous at x = 1.

recall.must_convey: That both pieces are continuous on their own intervals for any k, so only the joining point x = 1 gives a condition.
accept: each piece is continuous on its own side so only x equals one matters
the constant and the polynomial are continuous everywhere, only the join is left
check continuity at x equals one, that is the only point
rendu pieces already continuous, join daggara matrame check cheyyali
the only condition comes from the point where the two formulas meet

steps.why: This question gives the continuity and asks for k, so the single point where continuity can fail is the single place an equation in k can come from. Saying that is what earns the first mark.
common_mistakes: Trying to impose a condition at points other than x = 1.
Assuming continuity fails somewhere else because k appears in the formula.

steps.label: Write the two one-sided limits and f(1)
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Note which piece owns x = 1: the condition is x ≥ 1, so f(1) comes from k²x − k, not from the constant 2. Getting that wrong reverses the whole equation.
steps.memory_tip: The piece whose inequality carries the equals sign is the piece that gives the value at the join.
lines: Value at 1:   x = 1 satisfies x ≥ 1, so f(1) = k²(1) − k = k² − k
Right limit:   lim(x → 1⁺) f(x) = lim(x → 1⁺) (k²x − k) = k²(1) − k = k² − k

recall.must_convey: That the left limit is 2, and that f(1) and the right limit are both k² − k because x = 1 belongs to the piece x ≥ 1.
accept: left limit is two and the right limit is k squared minus k
f of one comes from k squared x minus k because one satisfies x greater than or equal to one
left side gives two, right side and the value give k squared minus k
left limit two, right limit k square minus k
x equals one belongs to the second piece so f of one is k squared minus k

steps.why: Writing all three quantities separately makes the next line a simple equation, and it forces the decision about which piece owns the point x = 1 to be made explicitly.
common_mistakes: Taking f(1) = 2 from the piece x < 1, when that piece does not include 1.
Reading the left limit from k²x − k instead of from the constant piece x < 1.

steps.label: Match the two pieces at x = 1
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The right limit already equals f(1), so the three-part condition collapses to one equation. Say that, rather than leaving two identical expressions on the page.
steps.memory_tip: Continuity at a join is one equation: left limit = right limit = value. When the value comes from the right piece, only the left limit is a new condition.
lines: f is continuous at x = 1  ⇒  lim(x → 1⁻) f(x) = f(1) = lim(x → 1⁺) f(x)
The right limit is already equal to f(1), so the only new condition is

recall.must_convey: That equating the left limit 2 with k² − k gives the quadratic k² − k − 2 = 0.
accept: set two equal to k squared minus k
equate the left limit and the value to get k squared minus k minus two equals zero
the continuity condition gives a quadratic in k
two ni k square minus k tho equate cheyyali
k squared minus k minus two equals zero
heard_as: two equals k squared minus k
k squared minus k minus two

steps.why: The equation in k is produced by the continuity condition itself, so this line is where the given information is actually used.
common_mistakes: Writing k² − k = 0 by forgetting to bring the 2 across.
Setting the derivative of the two pieces equal instead of the values — that is differentiability, not continuity.

steps.label: Solve the quadratic in k
steps.margin_note: Last mark. There are TWO answers and both are valid — no condition in the question rules either out. Checking each one back in f(1) takes one line and proves both.
steps.memory_tip: A quadratic condition usually means two answers; report both unless the question gives a reason to drop one.
lines: Check: k = 2 gives f(1) = 4 − 2 = 2; k = −1 gives f(1) = 1 + 1 = 2. Both match the left limit 2.

recall.must_convey: That k² − k − 2 = 0 factorises as (k − 2)(k + 1) = 0, giving k = 2 and k = −1, and that both are accepted.
accept: factorise to k minus two into k plus one so k is two or minus one
the two values are two and minus one
both roots work so give both answers
k rendu values, two and minus one
solve the quadratic, k equals two or k equals minus one
heard_as: k minus two into k plus one

steps.why: Both roots satisfy the one condition the question imposes, so both are answers. Substituting each back into f(1) is a cheap check that costs one line.
common_mistakes: Giving only k = 2 and dropping the negative root.
Factorising k² − k − 2 as (k + 2)(k − 1), which multiplies out to k² + k − 2.

insider_note: x = 1 belongs to the FIRST piece, so f(1) and the right limit are already equal and only the left gives a condition. That single equation k² − k = 2 has two roots, and both work.
